comments.text:
I believe the worst-case scenario is one in which Germany can no longer sell its products. Poland doesn't yet have the intellectual property or technological capabilities to thrive independently. We are still in the middle of the transition towards a truly high-income, knowledge-based economy that develops and owns patents.

Personally, I've stopped viewing the EU as a collection of countries and started seeing it as a collection of regions. Silesia, for example, has always been perfectly positioned.

In my opinion, the best thing that could happen is a fundamental change in how politicians view the EU. It is an absolute nightmare to navigate the AI Act, GDPR, PSD2, or virtually any IT project in the region because of all these regulations. You need an army of specialists just to bring a product to market, and each national market is simply too small in today's enormous global economy.

Nowadays, almost any serious European startup has to move to the USA to achieve global success. That's where you can find private funding, investors willing to take risks, and a business environment ready to support ambitious ventures.

Europe, with its many great countries, is simply too complicated and fragmented to compete effectively in this brave new world against China, India, and the USA, with their unified markets, legal frameworks, and government support. Individual European countries are just too small to scale businesses quickly enough.

Europe doesn't produce disruptors at scale. We have excellent universities, tremendous knowledge, and highly educated people, but the entire system is too fragmented.

Politicians like Trump are making this increasingly obvious.

From my perspective as a Pole, this is nothing new. For centuries, we lived in the shadow of Russia and Germany. The difference is that now Europe itself is being overshadowed by China and the USA, and potentially by India over the next 20–40 years.

Since 2000, France's real GDP has grown by roughly 35%, compared with more than 70% in the USA. Much of America's economic dynamism has come from Big Tech, disruptive businesses, and innovators. Europe certainly innovates, but it struggles to turn innovation into globally dominant companies.

And I won't even get into policy failures like ETS and ETS2, which were supposed to support green technologies but have, in my view, undermined the economic rationale for producing many goods in Europe. Meanwhile, Chinese companies have benefited from European technological know-how, particularly German innovations, and are now flooding the EU market with competing products.

It feels like nobody really cares about Europe's long-term prosperity. They just care about our money.

comments.author: @WitchKingofAngmarRides
comments.text:
The thesis that Poland is rising off a German decline actually isn't demonstrated in this video.  Indeed, what is presented is actually two parallel stories.  The German industries that are struggling, including chemical and automobiles, are not shown to be relocating to Poland, rather other industries are presented as rising.  Also not discussed is the huge budget deficits that Poland has been running for years, and the tens of billions of euros from the EU barely gets a mention.  Poland will have to reckon with the loss of EU money within a few years and find a way to repay debt that will become increasingly expensive to service.  In short, Germany still has great strength and Poland has some serious issues to address.

 A few comments on other responses to this video.  First, German contributions to the EU have been €20 billion more than receipts from the EU.  That is a huge amount of money that could be invested in German, but instead goes to recipient countries, including Poland, which has received billions more than it contributes each year.  Second, Poland has been running significant budget deficits; upwards of over six percent of GDP per year, and projected to be over seven percent of GDP in 2027.  Conversely, Germany has been debt-adverse, and even its less restrictive policy on debt spending is far tighter than what Poland is doing.  Third, while Poland has accepted immigrants, that has amounted to only 2.3 million people or 5.9 percent of its population.  By comparison, German has accepted 17.8 million people or 21.3 percent of its population.  Indeed, only the United States has accepted more immigrants that Germany.  While immigration can come with certain benefits, that also comes with massive costs which are borne by Germany alone.  Europe would have to come to a very different immigration policy without Germany's ability to absorb so many people from elsewhere in Europe, Africa, and Asia.

Comparing Japan and Germany highlights an interesting economic shift.

In the 1980s, the US pressured both manufacturing powerhouses to revalue their currencies, leading to a stronger Yen and Deutsche Mark.
Following this, and combined with the asset bubble burst, Japan moved much of its production to China, South Korea, and Taiwan. This allowed these Asian economies to absorb technology and experience rapid growth.
In contrast, Germany maintained a relatively undervalued currency through the creation of the EU and the introduction of the Euro. This allowed them to export tariff-free within Europe and keep their domestic manufacturing base intact.

Today, however, various factors are forcing Germany to lose its production base, which is shifting to Eastern European nations like Poland. This presents a massive opportunity for Eastern Europe. If they can successfully nurture their own domestic industries and companies—just as China, South Korea, and Taiwan did—they have a strong chance to become much wealthier.
Conversely, if they fail to develop their own industrial strength, similar to Southeast Asian nations like Thailand, their economic future could become highly challenging.

comments.text: Using percentage growth alone is misleading.
